7E1.full: 7 data bits, even parity, 1 stop bit
7E1.plain: Serial port settings: each character has 7 data bits, a parity check bit and a stop bit.

8E1.full: 8 data bits, even parity, 1 stop bit
8E1.plain: A serial line setting: each character has 8 data bits, a parity check bit and a stop bit.

8N1.full: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit
8N1.plain: A common serial line setting without the parity check bit. IEC 101 and 103 need 8E1 instead.

A-XDR.plain: A compact way to turn values into bytes, used inside DLMS messages.

AARE.plain: The meter's answer to a login request: accepted or refused, with the services it allows.

AARQ.plain: The first message of a DLMS session: it asks to log in and proposes the rules.

ABCD.plain: A number's four bytes sent highest byte first, in the order they are written.

ABP.plain: Keys and address set by hand in a LoRaWAN sensor, with no join.

AC.plain: The kind of electricity in the grid, which changes direction many times a second.

ACD.plain: A bit in an answer that says: I have urgent (class 1) data, please ask for it.

ACK.plain: A short reply that means "I got it".

ACSE.plain: The layer that opens and closes an association: a session between two MMS programs.

ADR.plain: Lets the network choose a sensor's data rate and transmit power from how well it is heard.

AE.plain: Part of a program's network name: the AE qualifier adds a number to the AP title.

AES.plain: A widely used cipher that turns data into secret form with a key.

AES-128.plain: AES encryption with a 128-bit secret key, far too long to guess.

AES-128-GCM.full: Advanced Encryption Standard, 128-bit key, Galois/Counter Mode
AES-128-GCM.plain: Encryption that hides the data and adds a tag proving nobody changed it on the way.

AES-CMAC.plain: A short code computed from a message with a secret key; only a key holder can make it.

AES-GCM-128.plain: AES encryption that also adds a check value, so any change to the message is noticed.

AHU.plain: The large fan unit that heats or cools air and moves it through a building.

AI.plain: An input that measures a value that varies, such as a voltage, instead of on or off.

allData.plain: The part of a GOOSE message that holds the values of its data set.

ANSI.plain: The body that publishes national standards in the United States.

AP.plain: The AP title is the unique name a program uses on the network to say who it is.

APC.plain: An IEC 61850 data type for a set point a client can change, such as a power limit.

APDU.plain: The BACnet message itself: the service and its data.

API.plain: The set of requests a program offers, so that other programs can use it.

APN.plain: A gateway of a mobile network. A private one keeps devices off the public internet.

APPID.plain: A number in a GOOSE or sampled-values frame that receivers use to pick the messages they want.

AppKey.plain: The sensor's secret root key; the session keys are made from it at each join.

AppSKey.plain: The key that encrypts the payload, shared by the sensor and the application server.

ASCII.full: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
ASCII.plain: The basic code that stores each letter, digit or sign as one byte.

ASDU.plain: The data part of an IEC 60870-5 message: its type, cause, addresses and values.

ASHRAE.full: American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers
ASHRAE.plain: The engineering society that publishes the BACnet standard, ASHRAE 135.

ASN.1.plain: A standard language to describe data, turned into bytes by rules such as BER or DER.

BACnet/IP.plain: BACnet messages carried in UDP datagrams, usually on port 47808.

BACnet/SC.plain: A newer BACnet transport: messages travel over TLS-encrypted WebSockets through a hub.

base64.plain: A way to write any bytes as plain letters and digits, so that they fit in text.

Base64.plain: A way to write any bytes as plain letters and digits, so that they fit in text.

Basic256Sha256.plain: A set of OPC UA security algorithms: 256-bit AES encryption and SHA-256 signatures.

BBMD.plain: Relays BACnet broadcasts from one IP subnet to another, since routers do not pass them.

BCC.plain: One byte computed from a message, so the receiver can spot damaged bytes.

BCD.plain: A way of writing numbers in which each decimal digit gets its own four bits.

bdSeq.plain: A number that ties an edge node's death message to its birth, one per MQTT session.

BER.plain: A way to write data as bytes: each item is a tag, a length and a value.

BI.plain: An on/off input, such as a contact that tells whether a breaker is open or closed.

BMS.full: Battery management system, or building management system
BMS.plain: Depends on the lesson: the battery's own guardian, or the computer that runs a building.

BVLC.plain: The small header of every BACnet/IP datagram: its kind and its length.

C-field.plain: The byte that says what kind of message an M-Bus frame is.

CA.plain: The trusted party that signs certificates. A device accepts only certificates signed by a CA it trusts.

CALL.plain: An OCPP message that asks for something and expects an answer. It starts with 2.

CALLERROR.plain: The OCPP answer saying that a request failed. It starts with 4.

CALLRESULT.plain: The OCPP answer saying that a request worked. It starts with 3.

CAN.plain: A two-wire bus first made for cars. Every device on it hears every short message.

CBC.plain: A mode of AES in which each block of data is mixed with the block before it.

CCITT.full: International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee
CCITT.plain: A former standards body. Its CRC formula is still widely used.

CCM.plain: A mode of AES that encrypts the data and adds a tag proving it was not changed.

CCS.plain: A common electric car plug that adds two large DC pins to an AC plug for fast charging.

CDAB.plain: A 32-bit value sent low 16-bit half first; each half keeps its high byte first.

CDR.plain: The final record of one charge: when, where, which card, how much energy, and the price.

CF.plain: The group of IEC 61850 attributes that hold settings such as units and scale factors.

CFG-1.plain: A PMU's list of everything it can measure. CFG-2 says what it sends now.

CFG-2.plain: A PMU's description of the data it sends: names, units, formats and rate.

CHK.plain: The CRC at the end of a C37.118 frame, used to spot damaged frames.

CI.plain: The M-Bus byte that says what kind of header and data follow.

CiA.plain: The association of CAN makers and users that publishes the CANopen standards.

CN.plain: The main name inside a certificate, such as the device's name.

COB-ID.plain: A CANopen frame's identifier: the kind of message plus the number of the node it belongs to.

ComplexACK.plain: A BACnet answer that carries data, such as the value read.

CON.plain: A DNP3 bit that asks the receiver to confirm that it got the message.

confRev.plain: A number that changes when a message's layout changes; sender and receiver must agree on it.

CONNACK.plain: The broker's answer to CONNECT: accepted, or why not.

CONNECT.plain: The first MQTT packet: the client's ID, login, keep alive time and will.

COT.plain: The reason a value was sent: asked for, changed by itself, sent on a timer, and so on.

COTP.plain: A small transport layer that MMS runs on, inside TCP.

COV.plain: A report sent when a value changes; for a measured value, only by more than a set amount.

CP.plain: The signal wire in a charging cable that tells car and charger about each other.

CP32Time2a.plain: A time stamp of milliseconds, minutes and hours, without the date.

CP56Time2a.plain: A time stamp from milliseconds up to the year, without a time zone.

CPO.plain: The company that runs public chargers and keeps them working.

CR.plain: A control byte (0x0D) that, with a line feed, ends a line of text.

CRC.plain: Check bytes computed from the message, so the receiver can tell if it arrived damaged.

CRL.plain: A list, signed by a CA, of certificates canceled before their end date.

CROB.plain: A DNP3 command for one output, such as trip or close a breaker with a pulse.

CS.plain: The frame's bytes added up, so the receiver can spot a damaged frame.

CSMS.plain: The operator's back office that runs the chargers, checks cards and records each charge.

CSQ.plain: A number that goes up with every challenge, so an old answer never fits a new one.

CT.plain: A transformer that scales a line's large current down to a small one that devices can measure.

DAN.plain: A device with two network ports, one on each of two separate networks.

DataValue.plain: An OPC UA value packed with its status code and timestamps.

datSet.plain: The list of values that a GOOSE message or a report carries.

DBIRTH.plain: Lists every metric of one device behind an edge node.

DC.plain: A steady voltage that does not alternate. A DC time code switches between two levels.

DCBA.plain: A number's four bytes sent lowest byte first: the reverse of how they are written.

DCMD.plain: A command from the host to a device behind an edge node.

DDATA.plain: New values of a device's metrics, sent by alias: only what changed.

DDEATH.plain: Says a device behind an edge node is gone.

DER.full: Distributed energy resource; also Distinguished Encoding Rules
DER.plain: Small power sources and storage, like rooftop solar or batteries. In data encoding, a strict way to write ASN.1.

DERControl.plain: An IEEE 2030.5 instruction to a device for a set time, such as limiting its output.

DevAddr.plain: The short 4-byte address a sensor gets when it joins, used in every later frame.

DevEUI.plain: The sensor's own 64-bit ID, unique in the world.

DevNonce.plain: A counter the sensor puts in each join request; a number seen before is refused.

DFC.plain: A bit that says the device is busy: wait before sending more data.

DFREQ.plain: How fast the grid frequency is rising or falling, in hertz per second.

DIF.plain: The byte before an M-Bus value that says how it is coded and whether it is stored.

DIFE.plain: Extra bytes after a DIF, for tariffs, subunits and higher storage numbers.

DIN 70121.plain: An older German specification for DC charging messages, still spoken by many cars and chargers.

DIR.plain: A bit that says which way a frame travels, for example from the master.

DISCONNECT.plain: Ends an MQTT connection cleanly; then the broker does not publish the will.

DLC.plain: The 4 bits in a CAN frame that tell how many data bytes follow, 0 to 8.

DMZ.plain: A buffer network between two others, where connections from both sides end.

DNP3.plain: A protocol for control centers to read and command remote stations, common in North America.

DPI.plain: A state held in two bits: 1 is off, 2 is on, 0 and 3 mean moving or faulty.

DR0.plain: The slowest LoRaWAN data rate; in Europe it is SF12 at 125 kHz.

DSCP.plain: A number in the IP header that tells routers how urgent a packet is.

DSO.plain: The company that runs the local grid that brings power to homes and businesses.

DST.plain: Summer time: clocks set one hour ahead for part of the year.

EAX'.plain: A way to use AES that proves who sent a message and can also encrypt it.

ECDHE.plain: A way for two sides to agree on a fresh secret key over an open network.

ECDSA.plain: A way to sign data with a private key, using elliptic-curve math.

EDS.plain: A file from the maker that lists every value a CANopen device holds, and its type.

EMCY.plain: A CANopen message a node sends at once when an error appears, and again when it clears.

EMIX.plain: An OASIS standard for describing energy prices and products, used inside OpenADR messages.

eMSP.plain: The company that gives drivers their charging card or app, and bills them.

EN.plain: A standard adopted by the European standards bodies, such as EN 13757.

EndDevice.plain: In IEEE 2030.5, the server's record of one device, such as an inverter.

EngineeringUnits.plain: An OPC UA property that names the unit of a value, such as kW.

EPSEM.full: Extended Protocol Specification for Electronic Metering
EPSEM.plain: The C12.22 envelope that holds table requests and sets their security.

EtherType.plain: Two bytes in an Ethernet frame that say what kind of message follows.

ETX.plain: A control byte (0x03) that marks where the data ends.

EVCC.plain: The computer in the car that talks to the charger.

EVSE.plain: One charging point: the part of a charger that charges one car at a time.

EXI.plain: A way to pack XML messages into very few bytes, used between car and charger.

FC.plain: A number that says what a frame asks for or answers, such as reset or send data.

FCB.plain: A bit that flips with every new request, so a repeated request can be spotted.

FCnt.plain: Counts the frames in each direction; the network refuses an old number as a replay.

FCtrl.plain: A LoRaWAN byte of flags: adaptive data rate, acknowledgment, more data waiting, options length.

FCV.plain: A bit that says whether the frame count bit counts in this frame.

FIN.plain: A bit that marks the last segment or fragment of a DNP3 message.

FIR.plain: A bit that marks the first segment or fragment of a DNP3 message.

FOptsLen.plain: How many bytes of MAC commands ride in the frame header.

FPort.plain: Says what the payload is: 0 for network commands, 1 to 223 for application data.

FR.plain: One of the seven areas of security in IEC 62443, such as identification or data flow.

FRACSEC.plain: The part of a C37.118 time stamp after the whole second, here in millionths.

FRMPayload.plain: The encrypted application data of a LoRaWAN frame.

FT 1.2.plain: The serial frame layout of IEC 101 and 103: start byte, length, checksum and end byte.

FUN.plain: The number of a relay function, such as overcurrent protection, that groups its signals.

GDOI.plain: A protocol that hands the same secret key to every member of a group.

GET.plain: The HTTP request that reads something from a web address without changing it.

GetNameList.plain: The MMS request that asks a device for the names of its objects.

GI.plain: A request for the current value of every signal a device has.

GO.plain: Marks a GOOSE control block in an IEC 61850 name.

gocbRef.plain: The full name of the control block that sends a GOOSE message.

goID.plain: A short name for a GOOSE stream that subscribers can check.

GOOSE.plain: A fast message one substation device sends to all others, used for trips and interlocks.

GPS.plain: Satellites whose signals also give a very exact time, used to set clocks.

GUID.plain: A 16-byte random number used as a name that nobody else will ever pick.

HDLC.plain: A way to frame messages on a serial line, with addresses and a check value.

HEL.plain: The first OPC UA message: the client's buffer sizes and the endpoint it wants.

HLS.plain: A DLMS login where each side proves it knows a secret key, without sending the key.

HMAC.plain: A fingerprint of a message made with a secret key: only a key holder can make it.

HMI.plain: The screens and software operators use to watch and control a substation or plant.

HomePlug Green PHY.plain: The powerline modem standard that car and charger use to send data over the control pilot.

HorWdSpd.plain: The data object for the wind speed measured level with the ground.

HSR.plain: Sends each frame both ways around a ring of devices, so one break loses nothing.

HTTP.plain: The request-and-answer protocol of the web: a client asks for an address, a server answers.

HTTPS.plain: HTTP inside an encrypted TLS connection: the secure web.

I-Am.plain: A device's answer to Who-Is: its number, message size limit and maker.

I-frame.plain: An IEC 104 frame that carries data, numbered so the receiver can confirm it.

IA.plain: The current in phase A of a three-phase line.

IANA.plain: The body that hands out the internet's official numbers, such as ports and organization numbers.

IB.plain: The current in phase B of a three-phase line.

IC.plain: The current in phase C of a three-phase line.

iCalendar.plain: The standard calendar format. OpenADR uses its way of writing start times and durations.

ICC.plain: Values in one partner's own domain on an ICCP server, which only that partner may see.

IDCODE.plain: The number of a PMU data stream. Sender and receiver must use the same one.

idToken.plain: In OCPP, the identity a driver shows to charge, such as the number of an RFID card.

IEC.plain: The world body that writes standards for electrical technology, such as IEC 60870 and IEC 61850.

IEC 104.plain: A protocol a control center uses to read and command substations over a network.

IEC 61850.plain: The international standard for data models and messages in substations and power plants.

IED.plain: A device with its own processor in a substation, such as a protection relay or a meter.

IEEE.full: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
IEEE.plain: A professional body that also writes standards, such as IEEE 1815 (DNP3) and C37.118.

IEEE 754.plain: How computers store decimal numbers in bits; a single-precision float takes 4 bytes.

IIN.plain: Two status bytes in every DNP3 answer: events waiting, clock not set, buffer full and more.

IKE.plain: The protocol two devices use to check each other's certificates and agree on keys.

IN.plain: The current in the neutral; zero when the three phases are balanced and healthy.

INF.plain: The number of one signal within a relay's function type (FUN).

InformationReport.plain: The MMS message a device sends without being asked, carrying values that changed.

IOA.plain: The address of one signal, such as a breaker or a measurement, inside a station.

IP.plain: The addressing that moves packets across networks: every device has an IP address.

IPsec.plain: Encryption at the network level, often used to build a VPN between two sites.

IPv4.plain: The common version of IP, with addresses such as 10.1.0.11.

IPv6.plain: The newer form of internet address, written as groups of hex digits, such as fe80::ff:fe00:a1.

IRIG.plain: A US group that defined standard time codes; IRIG-B is the one substations use.

IRIG-B.full: Inter-Range Instrumentation Group time code, format B
IRIG-B.plain: A time signal sent on a cable to set the clocks of substation devices.

ISA.plain: A professional body whose committee wrote the 62443 standards, published jointly with the IEC.

ISO.plain: A world standards body. Its network layers carry MMS and ICCP messages.

ISO 3166.plain: The international list of country codes, such as NL or NLD for the Netherlands.

ISO 8601.plain: The international way to write dates, times and durations, such as PT1H for one hour.

ISO14443.plain: The standard for contactless cards read at a few centimeters, as most charging cards are.

IT.plain: Office computers and networks: email, files, business software.

IV.plain: A starting value for encryption, so the same message encrypts differently each time.

JoinAccept.plain: The network's encrypted answer to a join request: an address and the numbers for new keys.

JoinEUI.plain: The 64-bit ID of the join server, which checks joins and makes the keys.

JoinNonce.plain: A counter the join server puts in each join accept, used to make new keys.

JoinRequest.plain: The message a LoRaWAN sensor sends to ask to join a network.

JSON.plain: A common text format for data: names and values between curly braces.

KDC.plain: A server that checks devices and gives every member of a group the same secret key.

LAN.plain: A network inside one building or site, such as a substation.

LE.plain: A simple, widely used profile of sampled values with fixed sample rates and eight values.

LF.plain: A control byte (0x0A) that, with a carriage return, ends a line of text.

LFDI.plain: A device's ID in IEEE 2030.5: the first 20 bytes of its certificate's fingerprint.

lFDI.plain: A device's ID in IEEE 2030.5: the first 20 bytes of its certificate's fingerprint.

LLN0.plain: The logical node that holds a device's common data and its control blocks.

LLS.plain: A DLMS login with a plain password, which travels unprotected.

LoRa.plain: The radio method LoRaWAN uses: it reaches kilometers with little power, but sends slowly.

M_DP_TB_1.plain: An IEC 104 message with the position of a two-state device, such as a breaker, and its time.

MAC.full: Media access control, or message authentication code
MAC.plain: On a network: a card's hardware address or the layer that shares the medium. In security: a check value made with a secret key.

MBAP.plain: The 7 bytes that start every Modbus TCP message: transaction ID, protocol ID, length and unit ID.

MHDR.plain: The first byte of a LoRaWAN frame: the message type and version.

MIC.plain: A few bytes computed with a secret key that prove a message is genuine and unchanged.

MMS.plain: A messaging standard for reading and writing named values. IEC 61850 and ICCP run on it.

MMXU.plain: The IEC 61850 logical node that holds measurements: power, voltage, current, frequency.

Modbus.plain: A simple, old and very common protocol to read and write values in industrial devices.

mRID.plain: A 128-bit ID, unique worldwide, that names one event, control or program.

MSG.plain: An OPC UA service message, such as Read or Browse, on an open secure channel.

MT.plain: A C12.19 table whose content the meter's maker decides, numbered from 2048.

MU.plain: A box next to the current and voltage transformers that measures them and sends samples on the network.

MV.plain: The IEC 61850 type for an analog measurement: its magnitude, quality and time.

MX.plain: The group of IEC 61850 attributes that hold measurements.

NBIRTH.plain: The first Sparkplug message of an edge node: all its metrics, with names, aliases and types.

NCMD.plain: A command from the host to an edge node, such as a request to rebirth.

NDATA.plain: New values of the edge node's own metrics, sent by alias.

NDEATH.plain: Says an edge node is gone; usually the broker publishes it as the node's will.

ndsCom.plain: A flag saying the sender's setup is not complete yet.

NetID.plain: The number of the LoRaWAN network operator; 0 means a private network.

NMT.plain: The CANopen messages that start, stop and reset the nodes on a bus.

NodeId.plain: A node's address in an OPC UA server: a namespace index and a number, string, GUID or byte string.

nonce.plain: A random or counting number used only once, so that an old message cannot be replayed.

NPDU.plain: BACnet's network layer header: version, control bits and, if needed, network addresses.

NTP.plain: How devices set their clocks from a time server over the network.

NULL.plain: An empty value; in BACnet, writing it releases a command slot.

NwkSKey.plain: The key the network uses to check that each frame is genuine.

OASIS.full: Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards
OASIS.plain: The standards body that publishes MQTT.

OBIS.plain: Six numbers that name a value inside a meter, such as 1.8.0 for energy taken from the grid.

OPC UA.plain: A protocol for industrial systems to exchange data, with built-in security.

openssl.plain: A free command-line tool and library for certificates, keys and encryption.

OPN.plain: The OPC UA message that opens or renews a secure channel.

OT.plain: The computers and controllers that run physical machines, such as a plant or a grid.

OTAA.plain: Joining a LoRaWAN network by radio: the sensor and network make fresh session keys each time.

P-256.plain: The most widely supported elliptic curve for key exchange and signatures.

PATCH.plain: The HTTP request that changes only some fields of an object.

PCS.plain: The large converter between a battery and the grid: it charges and discharges the battery.

PDC.plain: A computer that collects the streams of many PMUs and lines them up by time stamp.

PDO.plain: A CANopen message of live values, sent on a schedule or on change, without being asked.

PDU.plain: One message of a protocol layer: its header and its content.

PE.plain: The safety ground wire. Control pilot signals are measured against it.

PIM.plain: A routing protocol that tells routers where to forward multicast packets.

PINGREQ.plain: A tiny MQTT packet that says: I am still here.

PKI.plain: The system of trusted authorities that issue and sign certificates, so that devices can trust each other.

PLC.full: Programmable logic controller, or powerline communication
PLC.plain: An industrial control computer; in EV charging, data sent over the charging cable itself.

Plug & Charge.plain: Charging without a card or app: the car proves the driver's contract itself, with a certificate.

PMU.plain: A device that measures voltage and current waves, with exact time stamps from GPS.

POST.plain: The HTTP request that sends new data to a web address, such as a message or a record.

PP.plain: A pin in the plug whose resistor tells the charger how much current the cable can carry.

PPS.plain: A clock signal that marks the exact start of every second.

present-value.plain: The BACnet property that holds an object's current value.

PRM.plain: A bit that says whether a frame starts an exchange (1) or answers one (0).

protobuf.plain: A compact binary format for structured data, smaller and faster to read than JSON.

PRP.plain: Sends every frame over two separate networks at once, so one failure loses nothing.

PTP.plain: Sends time over a network and corrects each delay, keeping clocks within a microsecond.

PUBACK.plain: The receipt for a QoS 1 PUBLISH: the message has arrived.

PUBLISH.plain: An MQTT packet that carries a message to a topic.

PUT.plain: The HTTP request that creates or replaces the object at a web address.

PV.plain: Solar panels that turn sunlight into electricity.

QOI.plain: Says which signals an interrogation asks for: 20 means all of them.

QoS.plain: How hard MQTT tries to deliver a message: at most once, at least once, or exactly once.

R-GOOSE.plain: GOOSE carried in UDP over IP, so it can cross routers to other substations.

R-SV.plain: Sampled values carried in UDP over IP, so they can cross routers.

ReadProperty.plain: Asks a BACnet device for one property of one object.

REAL.plain: A decimal number in 4 bytes (IEEE 754 single precision).

REQ_UD2.plain: The M-Bus message that asks a meter to send its readings.

REST.plain: A style of web interface: each thing has its own web address, read and changed with HTTP.

RFC.plain: A numbered internet standard. RFC 1006 carries ISO messages over TCP.

RFID.plain: Contactless cards and tags, read by holding them near a reader, like a building pass.

RLRE.plain: The answer confirming that a session has ended.

RLRQ.plain: A message asking to end a session cleanly.

rms.plain: The effective value of an alternating current or voltage: what a meter shows.

RotSpd.plain: The data object for how fast the rotor turns, in revolutions per minute.

RP.plain: Marks an unbuffered report control block: changes during a lost connection are not kept.

RP002.plain: The LoRa Alliance document that sets frequencies, data rates and power limits for each region.

RptEna.plain: The attribute a client sets to TRUE so that a report control block starts sending.

RS-232.plain: The classic serial port of computers and devices, for short cables.

RS-485.plain: A common two-wire serial cable that links several devices on one line.

RSA.plain: A widely used public-key method for signatures and encryption, named after its three inventors.

RSP_UD.plain: A meter's M-Bus answer that carries its readings.

RSSI.plain: How strong a radio signal arrived, in dBm: closer to 0 is stronger.

RTU.plain: The box at a site that collects its signals and reports them to the control room.

RX1.plain: The first moment a class A sensor listens: usually 1 s after its uplink, on the same channel.

RX2.plain: The second moment a class A sensor listens: 1 s after RX1, on a fixed channel.

S-frame.plain: An IEC 104 frame that only confirms the data frames received so far.

SAv5.plain: The DNP3 security add-on that checks that critical commands come from the real master.

SCADA.plain: The control room's system that watches and operates the grid from afar.

SCL.plain: The XML files that describe IEC 61850 devices, their data and how they talk.

SDO.plain: A CANopen question and answer that reads or writes one value in a device.

SDP.plain: The car's first network message, asking where the charger's controller can be reached.

SECC.plain: The computer in the charger that talks to the car.

secp256r1.plain: The technical name of the P-256 curve, the most widely supported curve for keys and signatures.

SEQ.plain: A counter that ties an answer or a confirmation to the message it belongs to.

seq.plain: Counts 0 to 255 across an edge node's messages, so that a gap shows a lost message.

SF12.plain: The slowest common LoRa setting: longest range, but much longer time on air.

SF7.plain: The fastest common LoRa setting: shortest time on air, shortest range.

SFDI.plain: A short device ID a person can type: 36 bits of the certificate's fingerprint plus a check digit.

sFDI.plain: A short device ID a person can type: 36 bits of the certificate's fingerprint plus a check digit.

SHA-256.plain: A method that turns any data into a fixed 32-byte fingerprint.

SignAndEncrypt.plain: Every OPC UA message is signed against changes and encrypted against reading.

SimpleACK.plain: A BACnet answer that only says: done.

SIN.plain: An extra byte in an IEC 103 message. In a GI answer, it holds the scan number.

SL.plain: How strong an attacker a zone or product must stand up to, from SL 1 to SL 4.

SL-A.plain: The security level a zone really reaches, as built and run.

SL-C.plain: The security level a product can reach when it is set up correctly.

SL-T.plain: The security level a zone should reach, decided from its risks.

SLAC.plain: How a car's powerline modem finds the charger on its own cable, by comparing signal strengths.

smpCnt.plain: Numbers each sampled-values frame; it counts up and starts again at 0 every second.

smpSynch.plain: Says whether samples follow a shared clock: 0 means no; 1 or 2 name the kind of clock.

SND_NKE.plain: The M-Bus message that resets the link to a meter before it is read.

SND_NR.plain: A wireless M-Bus message a meter sends on its own, expecting no answer.

SNR.plain: How far a signal stands above the background noise, in dB; LoRa still works below 0.

SOC.plain: The whole seconds of a C37.118 time stamp, counted from 1 January 1970 UTC.

SOH.plain: A control byte (0x01) that starts a command message.

SP.plain: The group of IEC 61850 attributes that hold settings, such as set points.

spBv1.0.plain: The first level of every Sparkplug B topic.

SPDU.plain: In R-GOOSE, the session header; its number grows with every message, so old ones cannot be replayed.

sqNum.plain: Counts the copies of one GOOSE state; it starts again at 0 after each change.

ST.plain: In IEC 61850, the group of status values; in a North American meter, one of the standard data tables.

STALE.plain: A value still shown but no longer current, because its source has gone offline.

STARTDT.plain: The IEC 104 command that lets data start flowing on a connection.

STAT.plain: Two bytes of flags in each C37.118 data frame: data valid, clock in sync, and more.

STATE.plain: The retained message in which a Sparkplug host application says it is online or offline.

stNum.plain: Counts changes in a GOOSE stream; it goes up by one each time the data changes.

STP.plain: The byte 0xEE that begins every C12.18 packet.

STX.plain: A control byte (0x02) that marks where the data begins.

SUBACK.plain: The broker's answer to SUBSCRIBE: the QoS granted for each filter, or a refusal.

SUBSCRIBE.plain: Asks the MQTT broker for the messages of one or more topic filters.

SubscribeCOV.plain: Asks a BACnet device to report the changes of an object's value.

SV.plain: Streams of instant measurements of current and voltage, sent thousands of times a second.

svID.plain: The name of a sampled-values stream, set in the SCL file and checked by subscribers.

TAI.plain: The time scale of atomic clocks, without leap seconds; now 37 seconds ahead of UTC.

TC.plain: A network switch that measures how long it holds each PTP message and adds that to it.

TCP.plain: A reliable connection between two computers: data arrives complete and in order.

TLS.plain: Encryption around a connection, as in https: it hides the data and proves who is talking.

TotW.plain: The IEC 61850 name for the total real power a device produces or uses.

TPDO1.plain: The first process data object a CANopen node sends out.

TPKT.plain: Four bytes in front of each MMS message that give its length on TCP.

TR.plain: An IEC document that gives guidance but is not a full standard.

TS001.plain: The LoRa Alliance document that defines LoRaWAN frames, joining and security.

TSO.plain: The company that runs the high-voltage grid that carries power over long distances.

TTL.plain: A counter in an IP packet: each router lowers it, and at zero the packet is dropped.

TurSt.plain: The data object that holds the turbine's operating state.

U-frame.plain: An IEC 104 control frame, for example to start data transfer or test the link.

UA TCP.plain: OPC UA's small protocol on top of TCP: Hello, Acknowledge, then messages cut into chunks.

UDP.plain: A quick way to send messages without a connection or a delivery check.

UnconfirmedCOVNotification.plain: A change-of-value report that needs no answer.

Unix time.plain: Time counted in seconds since 1 January 1970, 00:00 UTC.

UNS.plain: A DNP3 bit that marks a message sent without a request.

URI.plain: A unique name written like a web address; it does not have to lead to a real page.

URL.plain: An address written as text, like a web address, that says where to connect.

URN.plain: A fixed, unique name for something. Unlike a URL, it is not an address to open.

UTC.plain: The world's standard time, without time zones or summer time.

UTF-8.plain: The common way to store text in any language as bytes.

V2G.plain: Communication, and sometimes energy, flowing between electric cars and the power grid.

V2GTP.plain: The 8-byte header in front of every message between car and charger.

VA.plain: The voltage of phase A of a three-phase line.

VAA.plain: The name a DLMS meter gives to the kind of session that is open.

varint.plain: A whole number stored in as few bytes as it needs, 7 bits per byte.

VAT.plain: The sales tax added to a price in Europe and many other countries.

VB.plain: The voltage of phase B of a three-phase line.

VC.plain: The voltage of phase C of a three-phase line.

VCC.plain: The part of an ICCP server shared by all partners, each allowed only what its table lists.

VEN.plain: In OpenADR, the box or program on the customer's side that receives events and acts on them.

VIF.plain: The byte that says what an M-Bus value measures and in which unit.

VLAN.plain: A tag in an Ethernet frame that splits one network into separate groups and sets a priority.

VN.plain: The voltage of the neutral; zero when the three phases are balanced and healthy.

VPN.plain: An encrypted tunnel between two sites across a shared network.

VSQ.plain: Says how many values an IEC 60870-5 message carries and how their addresses are given.

VT.plain: A transformer that scales a line's high voltage down to a small one that devices can measure.

VTN.plain: In OpenADR, the utility's or aggregator's server that sends events.

WAN.plain: A network that links distant sites, such as substations many kilometers apart.

WAPC.full: Wind power plant active power control
WAPC.plain: The logical node that sets how much active power the whole wind park may deliver.

WCNV.plain: The logical node for the power converter between the generator and the grid.

WebSocket.plain: A lasting two-way web connection, so both sides can send messages at any time.

WebSockets.plain: A lasting two-way connection that starts as a web request and passes most firewalls.

WGEN.plain: The logical node for the generator, which turns rotation into electricity.

Who-Is.plain: A broadcast question: which devices, in this number range, are out there?

WMET.plain: The logical node for weather data: wind speed and direction, temperature and more.

WNAC.plain: The logical node for the nacelle, the housing on top of the tower.

wPort.plain: A number in the DLMS header on TCP that says which client or which part of the meter talks.

WriteProperty.plain: Sets one property of one object in a BACnet device, optionally at a priority.

WROT.plain: The logical node for the rotor: how fast it turns, and its blades.

WTUR.plain: The logical node for the turbine as a whole: its power output and operating state.

X.509.plain: The usual format of a digital certificate: a device's ID card, signed by a certificate authority.

xDLMS.plain: The part of DLMS that carries the reads, writes and commands once a session is open.

XML.plain: A text format for structured data, with named tags in angle brackets.

XMPP.plain: A chat-style messaging protocol in which a server can push messages to clients at any time.

XOR.plain: A bit operation that flips each bit where the key has a 1. Doing it twice restores the original.
